title: Scale Significance
subtitle: Small causes are required by large effects

blocks.html: Astronomical scales are bewildering to human intuition. Billions of stars, billions of galaxies, and structure so large that measurements of distance and time blur together. A lightyear is often introduced as the distance a beam of light can cross in a year. To imagine that, we think of light speed—circling the Earth at the equator seven times per second, or reaching about three-quarters of the way to the Moon. And we expand that second into a year. This is a stretch for any human imagination.

But a lightyear is not even a distance in the way we commonly understand that term, as a length of space between two points existing at the same time. It was Einstein, in 1905, who broke open the secret that time and distance are specific to a unique three-dimensional reference frame. Hermann Minkowski followed his rationale to the conclusion that intuitive 3D space has no primitive existence at all. A division of spacetime into space and time arises only relative to a unique timelike observer.

And at large scales, the intuition really does break down. A lightyear does not act like a distance, but rather like a latency: the minimum time elapsed at point A before any signal sent from point B can be received.
